newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks plea with ADM on three products -source.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks plea with ADM on three products -source.

text.p: The Justice Department is pressing agribusiness giant Archer Daniels Midland Co. to accept a plea agreement that settles allegations of price fixing in three food and feed additives, a source familiar with the investigation said Wednesday.

As previously reported, the Justice Department is expected to file criminal charges in the three-year price fixing investigation Tuesday, and subsequently -- if a deal with ADM is reached -- announce a plea agreement settling the charges.

The investigation involves allegations that ADM and other producers conspired to fix prices of lysine, a livestock feed additive; citric acid, a food additive; and high-fructose corn syrup, a sweetener used in soft drinks and other foods.

The source said ADM and the Justice Department have nailed down most of the agreement involving lysine and the Justice Department now is pressing ADM to settle all three aspects of the case, the source said.
"The decision right now, even as of yesterday, is ... Justice is trying to push ADM to plead guilty on lysine, citric and fructose all in one," the source said Wednesday.
If a plea agreement is not reached, ADM could be indicted on price-fixing charges.

In addition to ADM, two executives -- Michael Andreas, vice chairman of the company and son of Chairman Dwayne Andreas, and Terrance Wilson, a group vice president in charge of corn refining -- will face some price-fixing charges, the source said.

Three companies, two Japanese and one South Korean, last month pleaded guilty or no contest to charges of price-fixing in the lysine market. The companies also agreed to cooperate with the Justice Department investigation.

When the probe came to light in June 1995, ADM said it was subpoenaed for documents and testimony on alleged price-fixing involving citric acid, high fructose corn syrup and lysine. Lysine has been the main thrust of the investigation.
ADM did not return phone calls requesting comment.
The Justice Department declined to comment.

A separate plea agreement between the Justice Department and Mark Whitacre, a former ADM executive who acted as a government informant in the antitrust investigation, is expected to be announced in October, the source said.
Whitacre, who headed ADM's BioProducts Division, was fired by ADM last year following allegations that he stole millions of dollars from the company.
Whitacre's attorney, James Epstein of the Chicago firm Epstein, Zaideman & Esrig, was on vacation and could not be reached for comment, his office said.

In addition to the U.S. government's antitrust investigation, Whitacre is also involved in a separate fraud investigation. That ongoing probe is focused on allegations that Whitacre and other executives at the company allegedly received bonuses from ADM through off-the-books payments.
ADM, however, has accused Whitacre and others of stealing the money, allegedly using phone invoices to channel the money into their accounts.
